title: Where the words point
source: Placement is our reading of each word’s definition, not a measurement, and the map places words, never people. Sources: aisafety.info, Nick Bostrom (1998 and 2002), Reid Hoffman on X (2025), the 2022 e/acc newsletter post, Morris et al. at Google DeepMind (2023), Vernor Vinge (1993) and Merriam-Webster.
hint: Hover, tap or focus a word to see what it means and where it comes from

points.label: AI doomer
points.method: Someone who thinks advanced AI is likely to end in catastrophe for humanity, such as human extinction or a permanent loss of control over our future.
points.reach: Older slang for a pessimist, applied to AI risk. Often a put-down from critics of the view; some who hold it use it for themselves.

points.label: X-risk
points.method: Existential risk: a risk that could wipe out humanity or permanently and drastically curtail its potential. AI is one candidate among several, alongside risks like engineered pandemics and nuclear war.
points.reach: Defined by the philosopher Nick Bostrom in 2002.

points.label: Gloomer
points.method: Someone who thinks we’ll be worse off with AI, without necessarily expecting catastrophe.
points.reach: One of four groups in Reid Hoffman and Greg Beato’s 2025 book Superagency, as Hoffman summed them up on X.

points.label: AI skeptic
points.method: Someone who doubts AI will be as capable or as world-changing as its builders and its critics expect.
points.reach: A plain word rather than a coined label. Skeptics can be worried about AI’s present harms or simply unimpressed.

points.label: AGI
points.method: Artificial general intelligence: AI that can do most of what people can. Definitions range from most tasks to most economically valuable work.
points.reach: A capability, not an outcome, so it sits on the center line.

points.label: Superintelligence
points.method: AI much smarter than the best human brains in practically every field.
points.reach: Nick Bostrom’s 1998 definition. Like AGI, a capability, so it sits on the center line.

points.label: The singularity
points.method: The point where superhuman intelligence changes the world so fast that what comes after can’t be predicted from here.
points.reach: Popularized by the science fiction writer Vernor Vinge in 1993.

points.label: Bloomer
points.method: Someone hopeful about AI who wants to push ahead while managing its risks.
points.reach: From Reid Hoffman and Greg Beato’s 2025 book Superagency; Hoffman calls himself one. Earlier, a meme for a cheerful young optimist.

points.label: Zoomer
points.method: Someone who wants AI built as fast as possible, without weighing the risks.
points.reach: The fourth group in Superagency. Not Gen Z’s “zoomer”.

points.label: e/acc
points.method: Effective accelerationism: the view that technological progress should be sped up, not slowed, because growth driven by technology and markets is good and can’t be stopped anyway.
points.reach: Named in a 2022 newsletter post by two pseudonymous X accounts, as a riff on effective altruism. It says what to do as much as how things turn out.
